section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Which statement best describes Native American societies in North America before sustained European contact?
options: A. They shared a largely uniform way of life
B. They copied the social models of Mesoamerican empires
C. They varied widely in lifestyle and economic organization
D. They routinely united in alliances against rival tribes
items.explanation: Before sustained European contact, North America held hundreds of distinct Native societies — from the pueblo farmers of the Southwest to the fishing cultures of the Pacific Northwest, the mound-builders of the Mississippi Valley, and the hunter-gatherers of the Great Basin. They spoke different languages, organized their economies differently, and lived in environments from desert to rainforest. No single way of life describes them; diversity was the defining feature.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Native societies were not uniform; they differed profoundly in language, economy, and social organization.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. North American societies did not copy Mesoamerican empires; they developed their own distinct cultures.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Native American societies varied widely in lifestyle and economic organization across the continent.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Tribes routinely warred and competed with one another; continent-wide alliances against rivals were not the norm.

items.stem: The map above shows the routes of Christopher Columbus's four voyages (1492-1503). Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the map?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Albert Bushnell Hart, 1906; pre-1930 publication

options: (A) Columbus's voyages were sponsored by the English crown to challenge Spain's Atlantic trade.
(B) Columbus's landfalls remained concentrated in the Caribbean and along the northern coast of South America.
(C) Columbus reached the Asian mainland during his third voyage.
(D) Portuguese navigators retraced Columbus's routes to found colonies in Brazil.
items.explanation: Columbus made four voyages between 1492 and 1503, and the map shows every landfall clustered in the Caribbean islands and along the northern coast of South America. He never reached North America or the Pacific, and he died believing he had found the edge of Asia. The map's pattern — repeated returns to the same island-and-coastline zone — defines the geographic limits of his achievement.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Columbus sailed for the Spanish crown, not the English; England did not sponsor his voyages.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The map shows Columbus's landfalls concentrated in the Caribbean and along the northern coast of South America.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Columbus never reached the Asian mainland; he explored Caribbean islands and the South American coast.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Portugal's Brazil resulted from Cabral's separate 1500 voyage, not from retracing Columbus's routes.

items.stem: The earliest peoples of the Americas
options: A. Moved seasonally following food sources
B. Built permanent towns and cities
C. Practiced settled agriculture exclusively
D. Arrived only a few centuries before 1492
items.explanation: The first Americans arrived during the last Ice Age, thousands of years before 1492, crossing from Asia and spreading across two continents. They were nomadic hunter-gatherers who moved with the seasons, following herds and ripening food sources. Permanent towns and settled agriculture came much later, in some regions only — the earliest way of life was mobile and seasonal.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The earliest peoples of the Americas were nomadic, moving seasonally to follow food sources.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Permanent towns and cities developed much later and only in some regions, long after the first arrivals.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Settled agriculture was a later development, not the practice of the earliest peoples.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The first Americans arrived thousands of years before 1492, not a few centuries earlier.

items.stem: Which of the following historical protests has the strongest continuities with the event shown in the painting? Pyle's 1905 painting above depicts the burning of Jamestown during Bacon's Rebellion (1676).

stimulus.pd_rationale: Howard Pyle, 1905; pre-1930 publication
stimulus.text_stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640

options: (A) The Whiskey Rebellion
(B) The Montgomery Bus Boycott
(C) Nat Turner’s Rebellion
(D) The Bonus Expeditionary Force March on Washington
items.explanation: Bacon's Rebellion (1676) was an armed uprising in Virginia by frontier settlers, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans against the colonial elite — the colony's poor taking up arms against established authority. Nat Turner's Rebellion (1831) continues that pattern most directly: another armed revolt in Virginia by those at the bottom of the social order against the ruling power. Both were violent challenges to Virginia's hierarchy from below.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Whiskey Rebellion was a tax protest by Pennsylvania farmers, not an uprising of the oppressed against Virginia's elite.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Montgomery Bus Boycott was a nonviolent twentieth-century protest, sharing neither the violence nor the colonial context.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Nat Turner's armed slave rebellion in Virginia most directly continues Bacon's pattern of violent uprising against established authority.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Bonus March was a Depression-era veterans' protest in Washington, not an armed colonial-era revolt.

items.stem: Colleges and universities during the colonial period were dedicated primarily to the training of
options: (A) medical doctors
(B) scientists
(C) political leaders
(D) the clergy
items.explanation: Colonial colleges — Harvard (1636), William and Mary, Yale, Princeton — were founded chiefly to train ministers. In a society where the church stood at the center of community life, an educated clergy was the most urgent need, and the early curricula were dominated by theology, Latin, and moral philosophy. Doctors, scientists, and statesmen were trained elsewhere or later; the colonial college was essentially a seminary with a broader curriculum.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Medical training was not the colonial colleges' purpose; doctors typically trained through apprenticeships.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Scientific training was minimal; the curriculum centered on classical languages and theology.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Training political leaders was not the primary mission, though some graduates entered public life.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Colonial colleges were dedicated primarily to training the clergy.

items.stem: Smith's narrative of capture and rescue best illustrates which early colonial pattern?

stimulus.image_caption: John Smith's Map of Virginia, engraved by William Hole, 1612 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1612, engraved by William Hole; Library of Congress, pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

"At last they brought him to Werowocomoco, where was Powhatan, their emperor. Here more than two hundred of those grim courtiers stood wondering at him..."
—Captain John Smith, on his capture, 1608 (abridged)

options: A. Immediate large-scale warfare
B. Successful mass conversion of the Powhatan
C. English dependence on Native peoples for survival
D. Peaceful, fairly negotiated land sales
items.explanation: Smith's famous tale — captured, about to be executed, then rescued by Pocahontas — reveals how fragile the Jamestown settlement was. The English could not feed themselves and survived only through trade with and aid from Powhatan's people. The story's real significance is what it admits between the lines: the colonists depended on Native peoples for their very survival.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The early years were marked by uneasy coexistence and trade, not immediate large-scale warfare.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. There was no successful mass conversion of the Powhatan; the story is about diplomacy and survival, not missionary triumph.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Smith's narrative illustrates English dependence on Native peoples for survival in the colony's fragile early years.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The passage describes a diplomatic encounter, not a fair negotiated land sale.

items.stem: The growth of colonial assemblies worried Britain for all of the following reasons EXCEPT
options: A. Assemblies holding the 'power of the purse' could erode British control
B. Assemblies spread democratic rule through the colonies
C. Assemblies sometimes defied instructions from London
D. Royal governors could barely restrain the assemblies
items.explanation: Britain worried about colonial assemblies because they held the power of the purse, defied London's instructions, and proved nearly impossible for royal governors to control. Those were threats to imperial authority. What did not worry Britain was the assemblies spreading democratic rule — the assemblies were oligarchic bodies of wealthy property holders, and Britain's concern was their growing power and defiance, not democratic ideology.

option_explanations.A: This did worry Britain, so it is not the answer. Control of taxation gave assemblies real leverage over imperial policy.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Britain feared the assemblies' power and defiance, not that they were spreading democratic rule.
option_explanations.C: This did worry Britain, so it is not the answer. Assemblies repeatedly ignored or defied instructions from London.
option_explanations.D: This did worry Britain, so it is not the answer. Governors struggled constantly to restrain assertive assemblies.

items.stem: The purpose of the Olive Branch Petition (1775) was to
options: A. To rally the colonies for war with Britain
B. To seek redress of colonial economic grievances
C. To ask the king to arrange a reconciliation
D. To request American independence
items.explanation: The Olive Branch Petition, adopted by the Second Continental Congress in July 1775, was a direct appeal to King George III to intervene and restore peace between Britain and the colonies. Even with fighting underway at Lexington, Concord, and Bunker Hill, most delegates still hoped for reconciliation within the empire. The petition asked the king to arrange a settlement — it was the last major attempt to avoid a complete break.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The petition sought peace and reconciliation, not a rallying cry for war.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. While grievances underlay it, the petition's purpose was to ask the king for reconciliation, not merely to list economic complaints.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Olive Branch Petition asked the king to arrange a reconciliation between Britain and the colonies.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The petition explicitly professed loyalty; independence was not its request.

items.stem: The British firing at Lexington on April 19, 1775, led to

stimulus.image_caption: Battle of Lexington, April 19, 1775 (after Amos Doolittle's 1775 engraving; U.S. National Archives).
stimulus.pd_rationale: After Amos Doolittle, 1775; U.S. National Archives
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 45-48 refer to the engraving above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. A controversial court case
B. A French invasion of Canada
C. Colonial uprisings against Britain
D. Collapse of the Sons of Liberty
items.explanation: When British troops fired on colonial militiamen at Lexington on April 19, 1775, the shot heard round the world ignited the colonies. Militia companies mobilized across New England, besieged Boston, and the Second Continental Congress soon took up the war effort. The firing transformed a political crisis into an armed uprising — colonial resistance became colonial rebellion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lexington produced war, not a court case; the legal battles came later.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. France did not invade Canada; it eventually allied with the Americans against Britain.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The British firing at Lexington sparked colonial uprisings against Britain across the colonies.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Sons of Liberty did not collapse; resistance organizations grew stronger after Lexington.

items.stem: Americans felt France finally treated the United States as a major power after
options: A. The Convention of 1800
B. Jay's Treaty
C. British seizures of American ships in the 1790s
D. The XYZ Affair
items.explanation: The Convention of 1800 (Treaty of Mortefontaine) ended the Quasi-War, the undeclared naval conflict between the United States and France. By negotiating a formal settlement, France dealt with America as a sovereign equal rather than a subordinate. After years of French seizures, insults like the XYZ Affair, and condescension, the convention marked France's recognition of the United States as a major power.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Convention of 1800 ended the Quasi-War and showed France treating the United States as a major power.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Jay's Treaty (1794) was with Britain, not France.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. British ship seizures humiliated America; they did not earn French respect.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The XYZ Affair (1798) was a French insult to American diplomats, the opposite of respectful treatment.

items.stem: Franklin most likely intended this cartoon for which audience?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The Colonies Reduc'd' (companion to Franklin's 'Magna Britannia: Her Colonies Reduc'd'), after Benjamin Franklin, published 1768.
stimulus.pd_rationale: After Benjamin Franklin, published by John Almon, 1768; British Museum, pre-1930

options: (A) Members of Parliament, whom Franklin lobbied to repeal the Stamp Act.
(B) Boston merchants organizing nonimportation boycotts.
(C) Pennsylvania backcountry settlers on the frontier.
(D) Members of the Sons of Liberty organizing protests against British policy.
items.explanation: Franklin published this cartoon in London during the Stamp Act crisis, and its audience was the British political class — above all Members of Parliament. The dismembered Britannia was a warning to the lawmakers themselves: your tax policies are tearing the empire apart, so repeal the Stamp Act. Franklin the lobbyist aimed his visual argument at the men whose votes could undo the damage.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Franklin aimed the cartoon at Members of Parliament, lobbying them to repeal the Stamp Act.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Boston merchants organizing boycotts were allies, not the audience Franklin needed to persuade.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Backcountry settlers were not the London-published cartoon's intended readers.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Sons of Liberty already opposed British policy; Franklin was trying to move Parliament, not preach to the converted.

items.stem: The situation described in the excerpt above led directly to

stimulus.text: “It is important for us, my brothers, that we exterminate from our lands this nation which seeks only to destroy us. You see as well as I that we can no longer supply our needs, as we have done from our brothers, the French…and when we wish to set out for our winter camp they do not want to give us any credit as our brothers the French do…. Therefore, my brothers, we must all swear their destruction and wait no longer. Nothing prevents us; they are few in numbers, and we can accomplish it.” Source: Chief Pontiac of the Ottawa, speaking to a war council, 1763

options: (A) the outbreak of war between Britain and France in North America
(B) the Proclamation of 1763 limiting westward settlement
(C) Parliament's passage of the Intolerable (Coercive) Acts
(D) the collapse of the French-British fur trade in North America
items.explanation: Pontiac's 1763 call for a united Native uprising against the British produced Pontiac's Rebellion — a wave of attacks on frontier forts across the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. Alarmed, Britain issued the Proclamation of 1763, forbidding colonial settlement west of the Appalachians to separate settlers from Native peoples and prevent further war. The rebellion's direct consequence was a new imperial boundary line.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The British-French war in North America had ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1763; Pontiac fought the British victors.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Pontiac's uprising led directly to the Proclamation of 1763 limiting westward settlement.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Intolerable Acts came in 1774, a decade later, in response to the Boston Tea Party.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The fur trade did not collapse; the proclamation was about separating settlers from Native lands.

items.stem: The cartoon above would most likely have found the strongest support among which of the following people?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The savages let loose, or The cruel fate of the Loyalists,' British cartoon, 1783 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1783; Library of Congress British Cartoon Prints Collection, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The cartoon above: 'The savages let loose, or The cruel fate of the Loyalists' (1783).

options: (A) A New England craftsman
(B) An Anglican minister
(C) A Pennsylvania farmer desiring western lands
(D) A member of the Virginia House of Burgesses
items.explanation: The cartoon defends British authority against colonial protest — the kind of message that resonated with Anglican ministers, who were among the most loyalist-leaning colonists. Tied to the Church of England and the established order, Anglican clergy tended to preach obedience to the Crown and view colonial resistance as dangerous disorder. A cartoon upholding imperial authority would find its warmest welcome among them.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A New England craftsman would more likely sympathize with colonial resistance than with a pro-authority cartoon.
option_explanations.B: Correct. An Anglican minister — tied to the established church and inclined toward loyalty — would most support the cartoon's pro-British message.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. A Pennsylvania farmer wanting western lands had grievances against British restrictions, not sympathy for imperial authority.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. A Virginia burgess belonged to the assembly tradition that increasingly resisted British policy.

items.stem: Women contributed vitally to the war effort because they
options: A. They financed much of the colonial cause
B. They wrote pro-resistance newspaper essays
C. They clothed the freezing troops at Valley Forge
D. They kept households and businesses running during the war
items.explanation: With men away at war, women kept the home front functioning: they ran farms and shops, managed businesses, produced homespun cloth to replace British imports, and sustained households under wartime hardship. That daily economic labor — keeping families fed and enterprises alive — was their vital contribution. The war effort depended on a functioning home economy, and women provided it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Women did not finance much of the colonial cause; large-scale financing came from loans and foreign aid.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Pro-resistance essays were written by men like Paine and Dickinson; women's contribution was economic and domestic.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Clothing troops at Valley Forge was one episode, not the broad vital contribution.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Women contributed vitally by keeping households and businesses running during the war.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the existence of political parties in the early United States?

stimulus.text: “Some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence, and deem them like the ark of the covenant, too sacred to be touched. They ascribe to the men of the preceding age a wisdom more than human, and suppose what they did to be beyond amendment…. But I know also, that laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind. As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816

options: (A) After the drafting of the Constitution, continued debates about states’ rights and competing economic interests led to the formation of political parties, such as the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans.
(B) Although Washington warned against the influence of political parties, he reluctantly accepted the endorsement of the Federalist Party.
(C) Political parties did not exist until the War of 1812, when Federalists asserted control over foreign policies with France and Britain.
(D) Two major political parties dominated early presidential elections until John Quincy Adams founded the Whig Party in 1824.
items.explanation: Jefferson's 1816 letter reflects on how institutions must change with the times — and the early republic proved him right. Debates over states' rights versus federal power and over Hamilton's economic program versus Jefferson's agrarian vision split the founders into Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. Parties formed not because the Constitution planned them but because real disagreements demanded organization.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Debates over states' rights and economic interests produced the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties after the Constitution.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Washington refused party labels and never accepted a Federalist endorsement; he stood above parties.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Parties existed from the 1790s, well before the War of 1812.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. John Quincy Adams did not found the Whig Party; it formed in the 1830s in opposition to Jackson.

items.stem: The American tactic Tecumseh condemns in the passage was

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, and Miamis, and you have taken our land from us... The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land."
—Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, 1810 (abridged)

options: A. Offering United States citizenship to Native peoples
B. Building mission schools for Native children
C. Negotiating land cessions with individual chiefs to break Native unity
D. Banning all trade between settlers and Native peoples
items.explanation: Tecumseh saw exactly what American negotiators were doing: approaching individual chiefs and villages separately to buy land cheaply, playing tribes against each other. His answer was pan-Indian unity — all tribes claiming a common and equal right in the land, so no single chief could sell what belonged to all. The tactic he condemned was divide-and-purchase: treaties with isolated chiefs designed to break Native unity.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Offering citizenship was not the tactic Tecumseh condemned; he condemned piecemeal land purchases.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Mission schools were not his subject; his grievance was the strategy of buying land from divided tribes.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Tecumseh condemned negotiating land cessions with individual chiefs to break Native unity.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Banning settler-Native trade was not the American tactic he described.

items.stem: Which group would have been most likely to circulate this cartoon?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1832, artist unknown (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed on Commons file page (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[An 1832 anti-Jackson cartoon shows President Andrew Jackson in royal robes and a crown, clutching a veto message in one hand while trampling the Constitution and the Bank of the United States underfoot.]

options: A. Southern planters who remained loyal to Jackson's administration
B. National Republicans and emerging Whigs opposed to Jackson's policies
C. Jacksonian Democrats who supported the president's program
D. Abolitionist societies campaigning against slavery in the South
items.explanation: The anti-Jackson cartoon — portraying him as King Andrew trampling the Constitution — was opposition propaganda, and its natural circulators were Jackson's political enemies: the National Republicans and the emerging Whigs. They built their identity on the charge that Jackson was a would-be tyrant destroying constitutional limits. Circulating such cartoons was how the opposition mobilized against him.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Southern planters loyal to Jackson would not circulate an attack on their own president.
option_explanations.B: Correct. National Republicans and emerging Whigs opposed to Jackson's policies would circulate this anti-Jackson cartoon.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jacksonian Democrats supported the president; they would not spread a cartoon portraying him as a tyrant.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Abolitionist societies focused on slavery, not on anti-Jackson constitutional cartoons.

items.stem: Critics of Andrew Jackson made all of the following charges EXCEPT that
options: A. He was a common man unfit for the presidency
B. He aggrandized presidential power
C. He lacked experience in public affairs
D. He governed through his 'Kitchen Cabinet'
items.explanation: Jackson's critics called him an unfit common man, accused him of aggrandizing presidential power, and denounced his reliance on the Kitchen Cabinet of unofficial advisers. The charge they did not make was that he lacked experience in public affairs — Jackson had been a congressman, senator, judge, and the nation's most famous general. Inexperience was the one accusation that would not stick.

option_explanations.A: Critics did make this charge, so it is not the answer. Elites sneered at Jackson as an unfit common man.
option_explanations.B: Critics did make this charge, so it is not the answer. The King Andrew image accused him of seizing power.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Jackson's long record as general, congressman, senator, and judge made inexperience an impossible charge.
option_explanations.D: Critics did make this charge, so it is not the answer. The Kitchen Cabinet of cronies was a favorite target.

items.stem: Parkman's description of the women's 'regrets' and 'apprehension' suggests that westward migration

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1868 by Currier & Ives. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)

options: A. Was universally celebrated by participants
B. Excluded women entirely
C. Imposed heavy emotional and physical costs on families
D. Was painless and quick
items.explanation: Francis Parkman's account of westward migration dwells on the women's regrets and apprehension — the dread of leaving home, the fear of the trail's dangers, the grief of separation. His description captures what the journey cost families emotionally and physically: months of hardship, illness, and loss. Migration was not an adventure for all; for many it was an ordeal endured with foreboding.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The women's regrets and apprehension show migration was not universally celebrated.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Women were central to the migration; Parkman describes their experience, not their absence.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Parkman's description suggests westward migration imposed heavy emotional and physical costs on families.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Regret and apprehension are the opposite of a painless, quick journey.

items.stem: Which of the following was the most important cause of the trend the passage illustrates?
options: (A) Congress shortened the naturalization period, rapidly enfranchising immigrants.
(B) Several major states extended the franchise to women.
(C) New civil-rights laws enfranchised large numbers of free African Americans.
(D) Most states reduced or eliminated property qualifications for voting.
items.explanation: The passage illustrates the great expansion of the electorate in the Jacksonian era — and its most important cause was the reduction or elimination of property qualifications for voting. As states dropped the requirement that voters own land, hundreds of thousands of ordinary white men entered the electorate. That democratization of the franchise, more than any other single change, created the mass politics of the age.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Congress did not shorten the naturalization period to enfranchise immigrants in this era.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Women's suffrage came decades later; it was not the cause of Jacksonian-era electoral growth.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. No civil-rights laws enfranchised large numbers of free African Americans in this period.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Reducing or eliminating property qualifications was the most important cause of the electorate's expansion.

items.stem: The cartoon's portrayal of Jackson trampling the Constitution refers most directly to critics' belief that Jackson had

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1832, artist unknown (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed on Commons file page (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[An 1832 anti-Jackson cartoon shows President Andrew Jackson in royal robes and a crown, clutching a veto message in one hand while trampling the Constitution and the Bank of the United States underfoot.]

options: A. Violated southern states' rights
B. Abused presidential power by defying Congress and the courts
C. Supported South Carolina's nullification claims against the tariff
D. Favored rechartering the Bank of the United States
items.explanation: The cartoon shows Jackson trampling the Constitution because his critics believed he had trampled constitutional limits in practice. They pointed to his veto of the Bank recharter, his removal of federal deposits against Congress's will, and his defiance of the Supreme Court over Cherokee removal. The image's charge is specific: a president abusing his power by defying the other branches.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon charges Jackson with abusing power, not with violating states' rights — he was accused of too much federal power, not too little.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The trampling image refers to critics' belief that Jackson abused presidential power by defying Congress and the courts.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jackson opposed nullification and threatened force against South Carolina; he did not support its claims.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Jackson vetoed the Bank's recharter; he was its destroyer, not its champion.

items.stem: The political changes visible in the passage most benefited which of the following?
options: (A) Andrew Jackson's Democratic Party, which mobilized the newly enfranchised voters.
(B) The temperance movement's political organizations, which lobbied state legislatures for prohibition laws.
(C) The women's suffrage movement.
(D) The New England Federalists.
items.explanation: The Jacksonian political changes — mass enfranchisement through the end of property qualifications — most benefited Andrew Jackson's Democratic Party. The Democrats built the first modern mass political machine, mobilizing the newly enfranchised voters with rallies, newspapers, and patronage. The expanded electorate was the raw material of Jacksonian Democracy, and the Democrats harvested it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Jackson's Democratic Party most benefited, mobilizing the newly enfranchised voters into a mass political organization.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The temperance movement's lobbying was a separate reform cause, not the beneficiary of electoral expansion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Women's suffrage was not advanced by Jacksonian enfranchisement, which was for white men.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The New England Federalists were the losers of this era, collapsing as mass democracy rose.

items.stem: Dix's later public service included

stimulus.text:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following excerpt.

"I come to present the strong claims of suffering humanity. I come as the advocate of helpless, forgotten, insane, and idiotic men and women... I proceed, gentlemen, briefly to call your attention to the present state of insane persons confined within this Commonwealth, in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience."
—Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843 (abridged)

options: A. Founding the American Red Cross after the war
B. Leading Union Army nurses as superintendent during the Civil War
C. Writing the antislavery novel Uncle Tom's Cabin
D. Leading the Seneca Falls women's rights convention of 1848
items.explanation: Dorothea Dix began as a reformer exposing the abuse of the mentally ill, but her later public service came during the Civil War, when she served as superintendent of Union Army nurses — organizing and overseeing the women who nursed wounded soldiers. She brought the same crusading energy to military nursing that she had brought to asylum reform. Her Civil War role was administrative and pioneering.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross; Dix's war service was leading Union nurses.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Dix served as superintendent of Union Army nurses during the Civil War.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin, not Dix.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott led Seneca Falls; Dix's cause was the mentally ill and then Army nursing.

items.stem: In the preface, Stowe's disclaimer of 'invidious feeling' toward slaveholders serves the rhetorical purpose of seeking to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1852 (first-edition title page). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The object of these sketches is to awaken sympathy and feeling for the African race, as they exist among us; to show their wrongs and sorrows, under a system so necessarily cruel and unjust as to defeat and do away the good effects of all that can be attempted for them."
—Harriet Beecher Stowe, preface to Uncle Tom's Cabin, 1852 (abridged)

options: A. Win over moderate readers by blaming the institution rather than individuals
B. Praise slaveholders as morally admirable people
C. Argue that slavery was economically efficient
D. Call for a violent revolution against the South
items.explanation: Stowe opens Uncle Tom's Cabin by disclaiming hostile feelings toward slaveholders as individuals — a strategic move. By blaming the institution of slavery rather than the people caught in it, she invited moderate Northern readers to condemn slavery without feeling they were being asked to hate Southerners personally. The disclaimer lowers defenses so the book's moral argument can reach readers who might otherwise turn away.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The disclaimer seeks to win moderate readers by blaming the institution of slavery rather than individual slaveholders.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Stowe does not praise slaveholders; she redirects blame to the system while still condemning it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Stowe argues slavery is morally indefensible, not economically efficient.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Stowe appeals to Christian conscience and moral suasion, not to violent revolution.

items.stem: Which of the following amendments to the U.S. Constitution provided the most federal legitimacy to the policy referenced above?

stimulus.text: “Some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907

options: (A) The 13th Amendment
(B) The 14th Amendment
(C) The 15th Amendment
(D) The 16th Amendment
items.explanation: Booker T. Washington's memory — a Union officer reading the Emancipation Proclamation and telling enslaved people they were free — describes a wartime measure. The Thirteenth Amendment gave that freedom permanent federal legitimacy: ratified in 1865, it abolished slavery throughout the United States and empowered Congress to enforce abolition. The amendment turned the proclamation's military emancipation into constitutional law.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Thirteenth Amendment provided the federal legitimacy that made emancipation permanent constitutional law.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) addressed citizenship and equal protection, not the abolition of slavery itself.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) addressed voting rights, not emancipation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) authorized the income tax, unrelated to emancipation.

items.stem: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation changed the war by

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published September 22, 1862 (preliminary proclamation). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) bringing the conflict to a swift close as the Confederacy saw its cause was hopeless.
(B) widening the scope of the war by prompting Great Britain to join the fight on the Union's side.
(C) provoking Jefferson Davis to vow massive resistance to emancipation.
(D) making Union war aims about more than preserving the Union.
items.explanation: Before 1863, the Union fought to preserve the nation; slavery's fate was undecided. The Emancipation Proclamation changed the war's meaning: it made the destruction of slavery an explicit Union war aim, transforming a war for the Union into a war for Union and freedom. That shift also kept Britain and France — both antislavery — from aiding the Confederacy. The war became about more than reunion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The war did not swiftly close; it ground on for more than two bloody years after the proclamation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Britain did not join the Union's side; emancipation helped keep Britain neutral.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Davis's vows of resistance were not the proclamation's significance; the transformation of Union war aims was.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Emancipation Proclamation made Union war aims about more than preserving the Union — it added emancipation.

items.stem: European powers withheld diplomatic recognition from the Confederacy because
options: A. Europe found alternative sources of cotton
B. Europe opposed the Confederacy's defense of slavery
C. Europe doubted the Confederacy could win
D. All of the above
items.explanation: European powers stayed out of the American Civil War for overlapping reasons: Britain found alternative cotton sources in Egypt and India, European public opinion opposed slavery, and leaders doubted the Confederacy could win a long war against Northern industry. No single cause explains non-recognition; it was the combination of economic adjustment, moral distaste, and military skepticism that kept Europe neutral.

option_explanations.A: This contributed, so it is not the answer. Alternative cotton supplies reduced Europe's dependence on the South.
option_explanations.B: This contributed, so it is not the answer. Opposition to slavery made recognizing a slave republic politically toxic.
option_explanations.C: This contributed, so it is not the answer. Doubts about Confederate victory counseled caution.
option_explanations.D: Correct. All of the above explain why Europe withheld recognition from the Confederacy.

items.stem: The policy referenced by the author above had which of the following impacts?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Painted 1864 by Francis Bicknell Carpenter (d. 1899); U.S. Capitol collection. Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus: “Some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907

options: (A) It declared that all enslaved people in the United States were granted citizen rights.
(B) It declared that all enslaved people in states in open rebellion were free.
(C) It declared that slavery in Union-held territories was illegal.
(D) It declared that slavery throughout the United States was illegal.
items.explanation: The policy in question is the Emancipation Proclamation of January 1, 1863 — a wartime measure that freed enslaved people only in the states in open rebellion against the Union. It deliberately did not touch slavery in the loyal border states or in Union-occupied areas, where Lincoln lacked the military authority and political willingness to act. Its impact was legally limited to Confederate-held territory.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The proclamation did not grant citizenship; it declared freedom in rebellious states.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in states in open rebellion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Union-held territories were explicitly exempted from the proclamation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Slavery throughout the United States was ended by the Thirteenth Amendment, not the proclamation.

items.stem: In the excerpt above, the reference to “the sanction of more erroneous religious belief” most probably refers to

stimulus.text: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860

options: (A) Southern Baptist justification of slavery on the grounds of white racial superiority
(B) the Puritan abolition of slavery in New England states
(C) Jewish slavery in the Torah
(D) Christian abolitionist rejection of slavery on moral grounds
items.explanation: South Carolina's secession declaration complains that Northern public opinion has invested a great political error — opposition to slavery — with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. The religious belief in question is the Christian abolitionist conviction that slavery is a sin: the moral, church-driven condemnation that made antislavery a crusade, not just a policy disagreement. South Carolina saw abolitionism as a false religion sanctifying a political attack on the South.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Southern Baptist justifications of slavery defended the institution; the declaration attacks the Northern religious belief behind abolition.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Puritan New England had abolished slavery long before; it was not the religious belief South Carolina meant.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jewish slavery in the Torah was not the contemporary religious force the declaration describes.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The phrase refers to Christian abolitionist rejection of slavery on moral grounds.

items.stem: Which other nineteenth-century movement used arguments most like Anthony's?
options: (A) The temperance movement
(B) Utopian communities
(C) The abolition movement
(D) The movement for publicly funded common schools
items.explanation: Susan B. Anthony's argument — that women are persons under the Constitution and therefore entitled to vote — mirrors the abolitionists' core method: appealing to the nation's founding principles of liberty and equality to condemn an unjust exclusion. Both movements claimed the Declaration's promises belonged to them too and demanded the republic live up to its own creed. The rhetoric of universal rights deployed against slavery was redeployed for women's suffrage.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The temperance movement argued about alcohol's harms, not about constitutional personhood and equal rights.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Utopian communities built experimental societies; they did not make Anthony-style constitutional arguments.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The abolition movement used the same appeal to founding principles of liberty and equality.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The common-schools movement argued for public education, not for voting rights from constitutional personhood.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT associated with the westward expansion of railroads during the mid- to late 19th century?
options: (A) The social doctrine of Manifest Destiny
(B) Increased confrontation between settlers and Western Native American tribes
(C) The economic decline and loss of political influence of Tammany Hall
(D) The emergence of the Populist movement
items.explanation: Railroad expansion was bound up with Manifest Destiny, intensified settler-Native conflict, and helped spawn the Populist movement among farmers squeezed by railroad rates. Tammany Hall — New York City's Democratic political machine — had nothing to do with western railroads; its power rested on urban immigrant votes, not transcontinental tracks. Its decline came from urban reform politics, not from anything happening west of the Mississippi.

option_explanations.A: This was associated with railroad expansion, so it is not the answer. Manifest Destiny sanctified the westward push railroads served.
option_explanations.B: This was associated with railroad expansion, so it is not the answer. Railroads brought settlers into violent conflict with Western tribes.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the NOT associated. Tammany Hall was an urban political machine unrelated to western railroad expansion.
option_explanations.D: This was associated with railroad expansion, so it is not the answer. Farmer anger at railroad power fed the Populist movement.

items.stem: Twain's anti-imperialism most directly continues which earlier American tradition?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Puck, 1899-01-25 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."
—Mark Twain, 1900 (abridged)

options: A. The Federalist call for a strong navy
B. The republican fear that empire corrupts liberty at home
C. The Southern defense of slavery
D. The Whig program of internal improvements
items.explanation: Mark Twain's anti-imperialism — his furious denunciation of American brutality in the Philippines — continues the old republican warning that empire corrupts liberty at home. From the founders onward, republicans feared that ruling foreign peoples would require the very standing armies, centralized power, and moral compromises that destroy self-government. Twain argued that an America that tortured Filipinos could not remain a free republic.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Federalists wanted a strong navy for national defense, not a critique of empire.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Twain's anti-imperialism continues the republican fear that empire corrupts liberty at home.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Southern defense of slavery was a pro-slavery argument, unrelated to Twain's anti-imperialism.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Whig program of internal improvements concerned domestic development, not the dangers of empire.

items.stem: The Turner Thesis
options: A. Echoed dime novels' romantic view of the West
B. Reckoned with the massacre of Native Americans
C. Stressed western expansion's effect on the American character
D. Emphasized the hardships of frontier settlements
items.explanation: Frederick Jackson Turner's 1893 thesis argued that the frontier — the meeting point of civilization and wilderness — forged the American character: its democracy, individualism, and inventiveness. The West mattered not for its romance or its hardships but for what it did to Americans. Turner's claim was about national character formed by the experience of expansion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Turner offered a scholarly argument about national development, not dime-novel romance.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Turner largely ignored the Native American catastrophe; reckoning with it was not his thesis.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Turner Thesis stressed western expansion's effect on the American character.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Frontier hardships were incidental to Turner; his subject was the frontier's shaping of democracy and individualism.

items.stem: The United States was able to annex Hawaii because

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1898 photograph (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: A. Queen Liliuokalani sought more American investment
B. Pro-American planters staged a revolt
C. Hawaiian public opinion demanded annexation
D. Hawaii feared other Pacific powers
items.explanation: American planters who dominated Hawaii's sugar economy overthrew Queen Liliuokalani in 1893 and established a republic designed for annexation. When the political winds shifted in Washington, their revolt made annexation possible: a pro-American regime was already in place, waiting to be absorbed. Hawaii was annexed because Americans on the islands seized power first.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Queen Liliuokalani resisted American domination; she did not seek more American investment.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Pro-American planters staged the revolt that overthrew the monarchy and opened the path to annexation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Native Hawaiians largely opposed annexation; the demand came from the planter elite.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Fear of other Pacific powers was not the mechanism; the planters' coup was.

items.stem: In the passage, Tarbell's argument against Standard Oil rests primarily on

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year... a sum which, if distributed among the thousands of stockholders, would make every one of them rich — and yet the company was built up by methods which have made it the most hated corporation in the country."
—Ida Tarbell, on Standard Oil, 1904 (abridged and paraphrased)

options: A. Interviews with John D. Rockefeller himself
B. Financial data on dividends, profits, and capitalization
C. Government statistics on consumer oil prices
D. Personal anecdotes about oil workers
items.explanation: Tarbell's attack on Standard Oil works by confronting the company's enormous wealth with the methods that built it: forty-five million dollars a year in dividends, yet a corporation widely hated for how it crushed competitors. Her argument rests on financial facts — dividends, profits, capitalization — deployed to show that the money was tainted by ruthless practices. The numbers make the moral case: such profits, gained such ways, condemn the trust.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Tarbell built her case from documents and financial records, not from interviews with Rockefeller himself.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Tarbell's argument rests primarily on financial data — dividends, profits, and capitalization — showing enormous wealth built by hated methods.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Government statistics on consumer oil prices were not her main evidence; corporate financial data was.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Personal anecdotes about oil workers were not the foundation of her argument; documented financial facts were.

items.stem: Urban machines like Tammany drew most support from

stimulus.pd_rationale: Harper's Weekly, 1871-10-21 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A Thomas Nast cartoon depicting Tammany Hall boss William M. Tweed as a bloated, grasping figure looming over New York City.]

options: A. Immigrants and lower-class voters
B. Federal patronage
C. Rural voters outside the city
D. The wealthier classes
items.explanation: Tammany Hall built its power on the votes of immigrants and the urban poor. The machine offered newcomers what they desperately needed — jobs, coal in winter, help with landlords and police — and in return received their loyal votes on Election Day. The wealthier classes despised the machine; its base was the tenement districts.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Urban machines like Tammany drew most support from immigrants and lower-class voters, trading services for votes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Federal patronage belonged to Washington, not to city machines; Tammany ran on local jobs and contracts.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Rural voters were outside the machine's city territory and its service network.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The wealthier classes were the machines' critics and reform opponents, not their supporters.

items.stem: To address the conditions in the table, Populists demanded
options: (A) a national sales tax.
(B) government funding for farm machinery.
(C) federal 'internal improvements' in the West, including railroads and canals.
(D) an end to the gold standard and coinage of silver.
items.explanation: The Populists' answer to farmers' distress — falling crop prices, crushing debts — was monetary: end the gold standard and coin silver freely. More money in circulation would raise prices and ease debts. Free silver became the movement's great rallying cry, the demand that defined Populism and carried William Jennings Bryan to national fame.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A national sales tax was never a Populist demand; their program centered on money and railroad reform.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Government funding for farm machinery was not the Populists' answer to the crisis in the table.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Federal internal improvements were an older Whig-Republican program, not the Populist demand.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Populists demanded an end to the gold standard and the free coinage of silver.

items.stem: Muckrakers furthered the causes of the Progressive movement by
options: (A) organizing grassroots campaigns for political reform at the state level
(B) suing large companies and donating their court awards to Progressive campaigns
(C) staging large, violent protests in support of Progressive goals
(D) alerting the public to the social ills and corporate corruption targeted by Progressives
items.explanation: Muckrakers — journalists like Ida Tarbell, Lincoln Steffens, and Upton Sinclair — served Progressivism by investigation and exposure. Their articles and books dragged corporate corruption, political graft, and social misery into public view, creating the outrage that made reform possible. They did not organize campaigns or lead protests; their weapon was publicity.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Muckrakers were journalists, not grassroots campaign organizers.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Muckrakers did not sue companies or fund campaigns; they wrote exposés.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Muckrakers did not stage violent protests; their method was investigative reporting.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Muckrakers furthered Progressivism by alerting the public to social ills and corporate corruption.

items.stem: Rural and small-town America in the 1920s would support legislation to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Cartoon by Rollin Kirby, 1925 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: A. Increase immigration from Eastern Europe
B. Require teaching creationism in schools
C. Ease penalties for bootleggers
D. Make deporting suspected radicals harder
items.explanation: Rural and small-town America in the 1920s was the stronghold of religious traditionalism — the world of William Jennings Bryan and the Scopes trial. Its legislators backed measures like requiring creationism in schools to defend biblical authority against modernism and evolution. The countryside's cultural conservatism expressed itself in laws protecting traditional faith.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Rural America supported restricting immigration, not increasing it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Rural legislators backed requiring creationism in schools, defending traditional religious belief.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Rural communities supported Prohibition enforcement; they did not want easier penalties for bootleggers.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Rural America favored deporting suspected radicals, not making it harder.

items.stem: Which of the following policies would be the biggest source of disagreement between the Progressive platform above and Populists of the 1890s?
options: (A) Laws designed to break up monopolies
(B) Laws allowing for direct election of senators
(C) Laws designed to create a progressive income tax
(D) Laws designed to nationalize the American rail system
items.explanation: Progressives and Populists agreed on breaking up monopolies, electing senators directly, and taxing incomes progressively — much of the Progressive platform was inherited from Populism. The sharp divide was over the railroads: Populists demanded the government own and operate the rail system outright, while Progressives preferred to regulate private railroads through commissions. Nationalization was the Populist demand Progressives would not adopt.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Both Progressives and Populists supported breaking up monopolies; this was common ground.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Direct election of senators was shared by both movements.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The progressive income tax was a shared demand.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Nationalizing the rail system was the Populist demand that most divided them from Progressives, who favored regulation.

items.stem: Which statement best reflects the cartoon's main point?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Judge magazine, 1899 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: (A) Overseas colonies betrayed America's founding democratic traditions.
(B) Overseas expansion was the natural next stage of American growth.
(C) Overseas colonies courted dangerous wars with rival empires.
(D) Overseas expansion was needed to civilize native peoples.
items.explanation: The cartoon presents overseas expansion as America's natural next step — the frontier spirit carried beyond the continent. After the West was settled, the argument ran, American energy and growth required new horizons in the Pacific and Caribbean. Expansion was not a betrayal of American traditions but their continuation: a growing nation growing outward.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon celebrates expansion as natural growth, not as a betrayal of democratic traditions.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The cartoon's main point is that overseas expansion was the natural next stage of American growth.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The cartoon does not warn about wars with rival empires; it presents expansion positively.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Civilizing native peoples was one imperialist argument, but the cartoon's point is about the naturalness of American growth.

items.stem: In the decades after the events depicted, the United States did which of the following?
options: (A) The United States retreated into multilateral alliances with developing nations.
(B) The United States withdrew from world affairs under domestic and foreign pressure.
(C) The United States deepened its economic and military presence in Latin America.
(D) The United States conditioned aid on human-rights improvements.
items.explanation: After the Spanish-American War era depicted in the cartoon, the United States did not retreat — it deepened its economic and military presence in Latin America through dollar diplomacy, repeated Marine interventions, and the Panama Canal. The decades after 1898 were the high tide of American hemispheric dominance. Engagement expanded, not contracted.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The United States did not retreat into multilateral partnerships with developing nations; it asserted dominance.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. America did not withdraw from world affairs; its Latin American presence deepened.
option_explanations.C: Correct. In the decades after, the United States deepened its economic and military presence in Latin America.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Conditioning aid on human rights was a later, post-1970s policy, not the pattern of this era.

items.stem: The activism Gilmore describes took place in the context of which of the following?
options: (A) Growing federal support for civil rights to burnish America's Cold War image.
(B) Southern industrialization bringing Black and white workers together.
(C) Military-led segregation in the Spanish-American War and World War I.
(D) The nadir of race relations — Jim Crow, federal inaction, and racism.
items.explanation: The activism Gilmore describes — Black organizing under Jim Crow — took place during the nadir of American race relations: the decades when segregation was law, lynching was common, and the federal government stood aside. Understanding the activism requires that bleak context: people organized precisely because the state offered no protection and the law offered no justice. The nadir is the backdrop that makes the courage legible.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Federal support for civil rights to burnish America's image came later, in the 1950s–60s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Southern industrialization bringing workers together does not describe the Jim Crow context of this activism.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Spanish-American War and World War I were earlier and different contexts.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The activism took place during the nadir of race relations — Jim Crow, federal inaction, and racism.

items.stem: How was the Red Scare in post–World War I America connected to organized labor movements?
options: (A) Unrestricted immigration after World War I flooded the job markets with low-wage workers, leading to resentment by union members and accusations of communist sympathies.
(B) California migrant workers were largely Italian immigrants, many of whom had anarchist leanings.
(C) Labor unions were largely thought to be controlled by liberals with Marxist sympathies.
(D) Senator Joseph McCarthy, a Wisconsin Republican, was hostile to both communism and labor unions, fueling suspicion among American Conservatives.
items.explanation: The post–World War I Red Scare fused fears of Bolshevism with fears of labor militancy: the great strikes of 1919 convinced many Americans that unions were covers for revolution. Unions were widely believed to be controlled by radicals with Marxist sympathies, so breaking strikes became patriotic and defending labor became suspicious. The Red Scare's connection to labor was the belief that organized workers were a communist front.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Immigration was restricted after the war, not unrestricted; the labor-Red Scare link was about unions' alleged radicalism.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. California migrant workers' backgrounds were not the mechanism connecting the Red Scare to organized labor.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Red Scare connected to labor through the belief that unions were controlled by liberals with Marxist sympathies.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. McCarthy's crusade was the Second Red Scare of the 1950s, not the post–World War I Red Scare.

items.stem: What was the most immediate consequence of the Korematsu decision?
options: (A) The military was ordered to compensate Japanese Americans for confiscated land.
(B) The military was ordered to close detention centers holding Italian and German Americans.
(C) The military was allowed to keep over 100,000 Japanese Americans interned.
(D) President Roosevelt proposed adding new justices to the Supreme Court.
items.explanation: The Supreme Court's Korematsu decision (1944) upheld the military's exclusion orders, and its most immediate consequence was practical: the government could keep more than 100,000 Japanese Americans confined in the camps. The ruling removed the last legal obstacle to continued internment. Justice would wait decades; confinement continued immediately.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No compensation was ordered; redress came decades later with the 1988 Civil Liberties Act.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The decision concerned Japanese Americans, not Italian and German detainees.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The decision's immediate consequence was allowing the military to keep over 100,000 Japanese Americans interned.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Roosevelt's court-packing proposal was 1937, seven years before Korematsu.

items.stem: What was the final result of the Vietnam War?
options: (A) The United States won a victory in the armed conflict and secured a democratic ally in the region.
(B) The United States withdrew and the nation became a single nation united under communist rule.
(C) The Vietnam War ended in a stalemate resulting in geographic division of the nation of Vietnam into democratic and communist nations.
(D) The Vietnam War has never ceased and armed conflicts between democratic and communist factions within the nation continue today.
items.explanation: The Vietnam War ended with American withdrawal and communist victory: after the U.S. pulled out under the 1973 Paris accords, North Vietnam conquered the South in 1975, reuniting the country under communist rule. There was no American victory, no permanent division, and no endless war — the war ended with a single Vietnam governed from Hanoi.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The United States did not win; it withdrew and its ally fell.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The United States withdrew and Vietnam became a single nation under communist rule.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Vietnam was not permanently divided like Korea; it was reunified by force.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The war ended in 1975; it did not continue indefinitely.

items.stem: The incident that began a chain of events that became one of the most infamous presidential scandals in American history and eventually led to the resignation of Richard Nixon was the

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-POTUS}}: official White House photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: (A) burglary of Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist’s office
(B) political sabotage of Nixon’s opponent, George McGovern
(C) illegal use of the CIA to hush up the FBI’s investigation of the events surrounding the publication of the Pentagon Papers
(D) break-in and attempted bugging of the Democratic Party’s national headquarters
items.explanation: The Watergate scandal — the burglary, the cover-up, and Nixon's resignation — began with the June 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex, where burglars tried to plant listening devices. Everything followed from that botched burglary: the investigation, the tapes, the articles of impeachment, the resignation. The break-in was the first domino.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Ellsberg psychiatrist burglary was a later Watergate-related crime, not the incident that started the chain.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Sabotage of McGovern was part of the dirty-tricks campaign, but the break-in began the scandal's chain.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Using the CIA to block the FBI was part of the cover-up, not the initiating incident.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The break-in and attempted bugging of the Democratic headquarters began the chain leading to Nixon's resignation.

items.stem: McCarthy's peak power and influence coincided with which of the following?
options: (A) The postwar wave of labor strikes in 1945–1946.
(B) The Korean War and its atmosphere of national-security crisis.
(C) The 'massive resistance' campaign of white Southerners against desegregation.
(D) The Cuban Missile Crisis.
items.explanation: Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist crusade reached its peak during the Korean War (1950–1953), when the conflict's stalemate, Chinese intervention, and fears of communist advance created an atmosphere of national-security crisis. McCarthy exploited that fear, charging that communists had infiltrated the government. His power rose and fell with the war's anxieties.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The 1945–1946 strike wave preceded McCarthy's rise, which came with the Korean War.
option_explanations.B: Correct. McCarthy's peak coincided with the Korean War and its atmosphere of national-security crisis.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Massive resistance to desegregation was a mid-1950s Southern campaign, separate from McCarthy's moment.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) came after McCarthy's 1954 downfall.

items.stem: King's imprisonment in Birmingham resulted from his commitment to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov}}: work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: (A) targeted assassinations of segregationist officials.
(B) massive letter-writing campaigns denouncing businesses that practiced segregation.
(C) armed self-defense against white violence.
(D) nonviolent direct action against unjust laws.
items.explanation: Martin Luther King Jr. was jailed in Birmingham in 1963 for leading nonviolent direct action — marches, sit-ins, and demonstrations deliberately violating segregation ordinances to force a confrontation with unjust laws. His Letter from Birmingham Jail defends exactly this method: breaking unjust laws openly and nonviolently to awaken the nation's conscience. The imprisonment was the price of the tactic.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. King rejected violence; assassinations were the opposite of his method.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Letter-writing campaigns were not what put King in the Birmingham jail; direct action did.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. King opposed armed self-defense as a movement tactic; his commitment was to nonviolence.
option_explanations.D: Correct. King's Birmingham imprisonment resulted from his commitment to nonviolent direct action against unjust laws.

items.stem: The cartoonist's central message is best described as which of the following?

stimulus.text: Image description: Herbert Block ('Herblock'), 'Fire,' Washington Post, 1949 — a political cartoon depicting a frantic figure directing an enormous fire hose at a tiny spark, a visual metaphor for the American response to the perceived domestic Communist threat after World War II.

options: (A) The Communist threat was so grave that only swift, severe government action could extinguish it.
(B) Panic over Communism was itself endangering Americans' civil liberties.
(C) Communism in the United States was a minor issue easily resolved.
(D) Americans had nothing to fear from the Communist threat.
items.explanation: Herblock's 1949 cartoon shows a panicked figure aiming a massive fire hose at a tiny spark — the visual argument that America's anti-communist response was wildly disproportionate to the actual domestic threat. The cartoon warns that the panic itself endangers civil liberties: loyalty oaths, blacklists, and investigations threaten free Americans more than the tiny spark of domestic communism does.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon mocks the overreaction; it does not call for swifter, severer action.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The cartoon's message is that panic over Communism was itself endangering Americans' civil liberties.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The cartoon does not dismiss communism as trivial; it warns that the response threatens liberty.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The cartoon acknowledges a spark of threat; its point is the response, not the absence of danger.

items.stem: The Tet Offensive demonstrated that

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-Military-Army-USACMH}}: U.S. Army Center of Military History photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: A. America was near decisive victory
B. Officials had not been candid about the war
C. The Vietcong could beat Americans in battle
D. U.S.–South Vietnamese cooperation was improving
items.explanation: The Tet Offensive of January 1968 — a massive coordinated Vietcong and North Vietnamese assault across South Vietnam — shattered the Johnson administration's claims that victory was near. Coming after months of official optimism, the offensive's scale proved to the American public that officials had not been candid about the war's progress. Tet was a military defeat for the communists but a political catastrophe for Washington's credibility.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Tet proved the opposite: the enemy could strike everywhere, undermining claims of near-victory.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Tet demonstrated that officials had not been candid about the war — the credibility gap.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Vietcong suffered devastating losses in Tet; they did not beat Americans in battle.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Tet exposed the weakness of the South Vietnamese regime, not improving cooperation.

items.stem: Carter's 1980 rhetorical approach most closely resembled that of

stimulus.text:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following excerpt.

President Carter's 1980 acceptance speech framed the election as a choice between two futures: one of pessimism, fear, and limits, and one of confidence in America's ability to meet its energy, economic, and foreign-policy challenges through shared sacrifice and renewed purpose.
—After President Jimmy Carter, Democratic convention acceptance speech, 1980 (paraphrased)

options: A. Hoover's philosophy of rugged individualism and voluntary cooperation
B. Coolidge's laissez-faire approach to business and the economy
C. Truman's 1948 appeal to Democratic values against the 'do-nothing' Congress
D. Harding's postwar call for a 'return to normalcy'
items.explanation: Carter's 1980 acceptance speech framed the election as a choice between fear and confidence, between limits and renewed purpose through shared sacrifice. That rhetoric of Democratic values against a do-nothing opposition echoes Harry Truman's 1948 campaign, when Truman barnstormed against the do-nothing Republican Congress and asked voters to choose active Democratic government. Both speeches made the election a referendum on Democratic purpose versus drift.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Hoover's rugged individualism rejected the active government Carter was promising.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Coolidge's laissez-faire was the opposite of Carter's call for shared national purpose.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Carter's approach resembled Truman's 1948 appeal to Democratic values against the do-nothing Congress.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Harding's return to normalcy promised rest, not Carter's call for sacrifice and renewed purpose.

items.stem: The 1984 Democratic ticket's selection of a woman for vice president most directly responded to

stimulus.text:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.
